phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial nasal [m], the same as English 'm'.
Long open-mid back rounded vowel [oː], marked by the acute accent for stress and length.
Voiced dental fricative [ð] (eth) followed by short close front [i].

pronunciation.approximation: 'MOH-thi' — hold the 'o' long like 'mow' without the glide, then say the voiced 'th' of 'father' and end with a short 'ee'.

pronunciation.note: Móði is Tier 1: the acute on ó and the eth (ð) are distinctive features the ASCII form loses, the eth preserving the Old Norse voiced dental fricative. The name is also the common noun for 'wrath' or 'courage', making the god an embodiment of the quality itself.

domains.title: Wrath, Son of Thor
domains.subtitle: The Angry God and Survivor of Ragnarök
domains.lead: Móði is the son of Þórr, the personification of wrath and courage. He appears in only a handful of passages, yet his role is consequential: he survives Ragnarök alongside his brother Magni and inherits their father's hammer Mjölnir. Where Magni is 'mighty,' Móði is 'fierce' — the emotional force that drives the thunder-god's line forward into the new world.

mythology.lead: Móði is not a god of independent myths. His entire dossier is a handful of verses: his name in a list of survivors, his place in a genealogy, and the skalds' habit of naming Þórr as his father. His significance lies in what he represents — the wrath that inherits the hammer — and in what his survival promises after Ragnarök.

myths.title: The Sons Who Survive
myths.text: The eddic poem Vafþrúðnismál asks the question every Norse listener cared about: who lives when the fire dies? Óðinn, disguised as Gagnráðr, puts it to the all-wise giant: what of the gods survives Surtr's flames? Vafþrúðnir answers (st. 51): Víðarr and Váli will dwell in the gods' holy seats when the blaze is slaked — 'and Móði and Magni shall have Mjölnir when Vingnir's war-work is ended.' Snorri repeats the list in Gylfaginning: Móði and Magni among the few who inherit the renewed world, the hammer passing to Þórr's sons. The stanza is nearly Móði's entire dramatic corpus — his name, his survival, his inheritance, in a single half-line. Its meaning is a Viking family's hope written cosmically: the work outlives the worker, and the sons keep the hammer.

myths.title: The Lifting of Hrungnir
myths.text: After Þórr kills the giant Hrungnir in single combat at the ford, the giant's corpse falls across him, one leg pinning the thunder-god's neck to the ground. The Æsir tug and heave in vain; none can shift the dead weight. Then Magni, Þórr's son by the giantess Járnsaxa — three nights old — toddles up, rebukes his father for such helplessness, and flings the leg aside as though it were light (Gylfaginning 51). Móði is named in the same genealogy as Magni's brother, though he does not act in the scene. Hrungnir had come to Ásgarð in a boasting match and challenged the gods to single combat, and Þórr's victory left him with a whetstone lodged in his skull — an ache the sorceress Gróa famously failed to charm away. Against that stubborn wound the tale sets its other lesson: pain in the father's head, impossible strength in the sons' arms. The story's function is to establish the impossible strength of Þórr's giant-born sons — and, for a careful listener, to foreshadow Ragnarök: the strength that lifts the dead off the father will one day lift the hammer off the grave.

myths.title: The Children of Þórr
myths.text: Snorri lists Þórr's children across his Edda, naming Móði and Magni as Þórr's sons by Járnsaxa, one of the giantesses (Gylfaginning; Skáldskaparmál 14), with the daughter Þrúðr among the children of Sif. Their names are the point: Mag-ni, 'Might,' and Mó-ði, 'Wrath' — the two halves of the thunder-god's power personified as an inheritance. Where Magni is raw strength, the word his brother embodies is the fierce courage that carries a fighter past fear, the same móðr that fills the skalds' verses. A god of storm fathering his own qualities as sons is Norse theology in its plainest form: Þórr's power is not a possession but a lineage, and lineages outlive persons. The sagas and poems keep the word in ordinary circulation — móðr names the fighter's surge in the heat of the press — so the personification runs in both directions: the god named for the quality, and the quality never quite losing the god.

myths.title: The Kennings Keep the Name
myths.text: Most of what can be said about Móði comes not from stories but from the skalds' grammar. Snorri's Skáldskaparmál (ch. 14) teaches how to name Þórr in verse: son of Óðinn and Jörð, husband of Sif, father of Magni and Móði and Þrúðr — and Viking-Age poets actually called Þórr by his children's names, 'Móði's father' standing for the god himself. The common noun móðr, wrath or courage, runs through the whole skaldic corpus as the word for what a warrior feels at the shield-wall. So Móði's afterlife is grammatical: he survives wherever a poet needs to say 'Þórr' in a metre too tight for 'Þórr.' It is a strangely fitting fate for a personified quality — a god whose whole mythology is his name, spoken inside his father's.

lore.syncretism: Móði has no clear non-Norse counterpart. His function — the personification of wrath or courage — resembles other Indo-European personified forces, such as the Greek Thumos or the Roman Furor, but he is specifically embedded in the genealogy of Þórr. His survival after Ragnarök places him in the small company of gods who bridge the old world and the new. In modern retellings he is often overshadowed by his brother Magni and his father Þórr, but his name preserves an important Norse idea: that wrath, rightly directed, is a form of power.
lore.culturalLegacy: Móði remains a minor figure in popular reception, usually appearing as Magni's brother or as one of the survivors of Ragnarök. In video games, comics, and modern Heathenry, he is sometimes developed as a god of berserk courage or youthful fury. His inheritance of Mjölnir alongside Magni is a favorite detail in retellings of the end of the world: the thunder does not cease; it is passed to the next generation. For psychologists and poets, his name is a reminder that wrath and courage are etymologically and mythologically intertwined in Norse thought.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Móði is the anger that survives. He does not have his father's epic battles or his brother's astonishing strength; what he has is the fury that keeps going after the world ends. In a pantheon full of larger-than-life actors, he is a small but necessary figure: the emotion that outlives the body.

The survival of Móði and Magni suggests that Þórr's power is not only physical but emotional. Might and wrath together inherit the hammer. The new world will need both: the strength to rebuild and the fire to protect what is rebuilt. Móði is that fire, banked but not extinguished, waiting for the next age.

lore.archaeology: No archaeological find names Móði directly; his existence rests on the medieval manuscript tradition — the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270) and Snorri's Prose Edda (c. 1220). But his world is richly material: tens of thousands of Viking-Age Mjöllnir pendants, from Iceland to Russia, attest the hammer cult his myth inherits, and the picture-stones and rune-stones of Gotland and Sweden preserve the thunder-god's exploits that frame his sons' fame. The broader context — the warrior ethos that made móðr, battle-courage, a quality worth deifying — is documented across the whole material culture of Scandinavian heathendom.
lore.cult: No cult of Móði is attested, and none should be invented. The sources give him no sanctuary, no festival, no priesthood, no place-name; his name appears on no runestone and in no oath-formula. What he had was a family: as son of Þórr he shared in the thunder-god's enormous household religion — the hammer amulets, the hallowing sign, the thunder lore — but nowhere as anything more than an inheritor named in poetry. If any veneration touched him, it was as part of that household, the way a saga genealogy names a lineage rather than a congregation. His real cult is linguistic: móðr, the everyday Old Norse word for wrath and courage, spoken every time a skald praised battle-fury — the god dissolved into the noun he personified.
lore.iconography: No surviving image names Móði, and Viking-Age art gives Þórr's sons no secure portrait. His attributes are entirely textual, and they amount to two: inheritance and fury. Vafþrúðnismál hands him Mjöllnir at the renewal of the world, so the hammer is his by right — the very pendant shape that hung from ten thousand necks, though none of them meant him. In the family lists he stands beside Magni, 'the strong one', as 'the fierce one', a pairing that says his portrait was the face of battle-anger itself. Later book illustration froze a type — the young warrior at his father's side — but that is a nineteenth-century inheritance of the Edda revival, not a medieval likeness. Medieval Móði lived in the verse: a name in a genealogy and a hammer's next owner.
lore.reception: Móði's afterlife is philology's afterlife. In the medieval manuscripts he is a supporting name — Vafþrúðnismál's line about Mjöllnir's inheritance, Snorri's genealogies — and so he stayed until print antiquarianism gave the Eddas to Europe in 1787 and the Romantic century found the idea of personified wrath irresistible. Jacob Grimm, in the Deutsche Mythologie, set the frame that still governs: Móðr and Magni, Wrath and Might, as living fossils of a mythology that could make gods out of qualities. The great dictionaries then canonized the word — Cleasby–Vigfusson's 1874 entry for móðr walks the reader from common noun to god and back — and the modern handbooks, Simek and Lindow, give him their sober two paragraphs. His name's cognates still hum beneath the living languages: English 'mood' and German 'Mut' belong to the same family of temper-words, showing what he was before he was anyone's son. Modern retellings promote him to Ragnarök's survivor-in-chief; the deeper survival is lexical — a god who never needed believers to be remembered, because speakers never stopped saying his name.
